questions.stem_markdown: In a Sydney adolescent clinic, a 17-year-old clearly understands a recommended non-urgent treatment, can explain the main risks and longer-term consequences, and wants to proceed. Her mother says, "Because she is under 18, my consent is still required." What is the **best response** based on the notes?

options.text: Parental consent is always required for anyone under 18
When understanding is mature, the young person’s consent is usually sufficient
Consent can only proceed if both the parent and another adult relative agree
Treatment should wait until the young person turns 18
A young person’s consent only matters in an emergency

questions.explanation_markdown: The consent table in the notes states that with **mature understanding**, the **consent of the young person is usually sufficient**. This is different from saying parents are irrelevant in all situations, but it does mean parental consent is not automatically required simply because the patient is under 18.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not say that parental consent is always required for every minor.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not create this requirement.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not recommend delaying appropriate treatment until adulthood when a young person has mature understanding.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes distinguish emergency treatment from ordinary consent; they do not limit young-person consent to emergencies only.

key_takeaways: Mature understanding changes the consent pathway for minors.
The notes state that a young person’s consent is usually sufficient when understanding is mature.
Parental involvement and parental legal necessity are not always the same thing.

questions.stem_markdown: During a consent discussion for a non-urgent procedure, a 16-year-old gives a clear answer when alone but changes position completely whenever one parent enters the room and cannot explain the change. Which concern from the notes is **most relevant** when assessing competence?

options.text: Limited school performance
Inability to manage influences on decision-making
Being younger than 18 years
Lack of previous hospital admission
Not having a Medicare card

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that legal competence to consent includes the minor’s **ability to manage influences on decision-making**. A young person who cannot hold or explain a decision under pressure raises concern in that specific area.

why_others_wrong.A: School performance is not the specific consent criterion highlighted in this scenario.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not use minority alone as the determining factor for competence.
why_others_wrong.D: Previous hospital admission is not listed as a criterion for competence in the notes.
why_others_wrong.E: Medicare access is unrelated to the capacity concern being assessed here.

key_takeaways: Consent assessment includes how well a young person manages outside influence.
Capacity concerns can appear even when basic factual understanding seems present.
The notes list influence-management as a specific competence factor.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old and parents disagree about whether the young person truly understands the proposed treatment. The main uncertainty is the adolescent’s **decision-making capacity**, not the medical plan itself. According to the notes, what is the **best additional step**?

options.text: Obtain specialist opinion on the minor’s capacity
Seek a second medical opinion on the treatment plan
Make a Mandatory Report immediately
Proceed without any consent because there is disagreement
Delay further discussion until the family returns with another relative

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes list **obtaining specialist opinion on the minor’s capacity (if applicable)** as one of the steps to consider when there is refusal or conflict. That is the best fit when the disagreement is specifically about the young person’s capacity rather than the treatment plan itself.

why_others_wrong.B: A second medical opinion is the listed step when the dispute is about the treatment plan, not primarily about capacity.
why_others_wrong.C: A Mandatory Report is mentioned when refusal creates risk of significant harm, which is not the main issue described here.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not support ignoring consent requirements because disagreement exists.
why_others_wrong.E: This is not one of the structured steps listed in the source material.

key_takeaways: The notes distinguish disagreement about capacity from disagreement about the treatment plan.
Capacity concerns can prompt specialist opinion on the young person’s decision-making ability.
Conflict resolution should be matched to the actual source of the dispute.

questions.stem_markdown: In a NSW paediatric service, the family and treating team all accept that a 16-year-old understands the situation well, but there is a major dispute about the **recommended treatment plan itself**. According to the notes, what is the **best next step**?

options.text: Obtain specialist opinion on the minor’s capacity
Make a Mandatory Report
Proceed with the parents’ preferred plan without further review
Seek a second medical opinion
Treat the disagreement as legally irrelevant because the young person has capacity

questions.explanation_markdown: The refusal/conflict section in the notes states that if there is a **dispute about the treatment plan**, clinicians should **seek a second medical opinion**. This is different from obtaining specialist opinion on capacity.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the better fit when the dispute is about the young person’s capacity rather than the treatment plan.
why_others_wrong.B: The notes reserve Mandatory Report consideration for situations involving risk of significant harm due to parental refusal.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not support bypassing review when the treatment plan itself is disputed.
why_others_wrong.E: Capacity does not make a major treatment-plan dispute disappear; the notes still outline additional steps.

key_takeaways: The notes separate disputes about capacity from disputes about the treatment plan.
A second medical opinion is the listed response to treatment-plan disagreement.
Applied consent questions often turn on what exactly is being disputed.

questions.stem_markdown: A registrar says that once a 16-year-old agrees to a confidential alcohol and drug assessment, the team should keep the discussion narrow and avoid exploring anything else. Which response is **most consistent** with the notes?

options.text: Correct, because confidentiality means broader risk assessment should stop
Incorrect, because comprehensive adolescent assessment still includes identifying risks and addressing child protection issues
Correct, but only if CRAFFT screening is negative
Incorrect, because parents must answer all sensitive questions instead
Correct, because confidentiality only applies to substance use questions

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that comprehensive adolescent drug and alcohol assessment includes **engagement and discussion of confidentiality**, but also **identifying risks and addressing child protection issues**. why_others_wrong.A: The source material explicitly includes broader risk identification and child protection within the assessment.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not say that a negative screening result removes the need for broader risk thinking.
why_others_wrong.D: The source material does not make the parent the required source for all sensitive questioning.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not restrict confidentiality to a single narrow question type.

key_takeaways: Confidentiality supports adolescent engagement but does not replace risk assessment.
The notes link adolescent assessment with both confidentiality and child protection awareness.
A focused substance-use history still sits inside a broader safety framework.

why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not suggest forcing an immediate solo decision from the young person in this situation.

Delay itself can become clinically important and should be addressed clearly.
Conflict management is not just about formal legal steps.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old is being considered for a treatment course that would involve administering a **drug of addiction for more than 10 days**. What is the **most important implication** for the consent pathway based on the notes?

options.text: Ordinary parental consent is sufficient if the young person agrees
If the young person is Gillick competent, their consent alone is enough
This is special medical treatment and requires consent from the Guardianship Division of NCAT
Emergency treatment provisions automatically apply
The decision depends only on whether the family has a Medicare Safety Net

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes list treatment that **involves administering a drug of addiction for more than 10 days** as **special medical treatment** for those under 16 years old. They also state that **consent from the Guardianship Division of NCAT is required**, and that neither the parent nor the mature minor can consent.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes state that ordinary parental consent is not enough for this special medical treatment category.
why_others_wrong.B: The source material says a mature minor cannot consent to this category either.
why_others_wrong.D: The emergency exception is a separate concept and is not triggered simply by this treatment type.
why_others_wrong.E: Medicare arrangements do not determine the special medical treatment consent pathway.

key_takeaways: Drug-of-addiction treatment beyond 10 days is specifically listed as special medical treatment in the notes.
Special medical treatment changes the usual consent pathway.
Ordinary parental consent and mature-minor consent are not sufficient for this category.

Adolescent Medicare arrangements can support more independent access because a young person may have their own card and online claims history is controlled by the adolescent rather than the parent
A young person may have their own card, but online Medicare claims history must remain parent-controlled
Medicare arrangements only affect hospital admissions, not outpatient or GP access
Medicare access changes during adolescence do not affect privacy or independent healthcare use

why_others_wrong.A: The notes describe adolescent Medicare changes rather than requiring total dependence on parents until adulthood.

why_others_wrong.D: The notes do not restrict these Medicare arrangements to hospital care only.
why_others_wrong.E: The source material clearly describes Medicare changes that affect adolescent access and privacy.

key_takeaways: The notes include Medicare changes that matter for adolescent independence in healthcare.
Service access questions are an important part of adolescent care.
Privacy and practical access can both be shaped by how Medicare arrangements change during adolescence.
